name: PHAT

lead: PHAT is a lifting program created by Layne Norton, a natural bodybuilder and powerlifter with a PhD in nutritional sciences. It combines heavy low-rep training with higher-rep bodybuilding work so each muscle is trained twice a week in different ways.
People use it to add muscle size and strength, which changes shoulders, back, chest, arms and legs, the physique side of appearance.

paras: The standard week has an upper-body power day, a lower-body power day, then back and shoulder, lower-body, and chest and arms hypertrophy days, with two rest days. Power days use heavy compounds at low reps with long rests; hypertrophy days use moderate to high reps with shorter rests [2][3].

Sources describe it as demanding, with sessions of 75 to 120 minutes and roughly 8 to 12 hours a week, and advise against it for beginners or those with limited gym access or recovery [2][3]. Overuse injury is the main practical risk of high-volume training.

chain: More muscle size across the body
angle.text: PHAT is a structured way to gain muscle, which improves shoulders, back, chest, arms and legs, so the visual benefit is a more muscular physique.

lead: PHAT, short for Power Hypertrophy Adaptive Training, is a five-day powerbuilding split created and popularized by Layne Norton, a natural bodybuilder and powerlifter with a doctorate in nutritional sciences [1]. It blends strength-focused and size-focused training in one week.

People use PHAT to build muscle mass and strength. Training each muscle group twice per week, once with heavy loads and once with higher volume, is aimed at a bigger, more developed physique [1][2]. The program circulates on looksmax.org, where a thread presents it as a gym program for thin lifters [3].

paras: The standard template is upper power, lower power, rest, back and shoulders hypertrophy, lower hypertrophy, chest and arms hypertrophy, rest [1][2].

Power days use heavy compound lifts, about 3-5 sets of 3-5 reps with long rests. Hypertrophy days use about 6-20 reps, with speed work on lighter loads, shorter rests and more isolation work [1][2]. A four-day variation merges the upper hypertrophy days [1].

Reviewers describe PHAT as not a beginner program and as needing a well-equipped gym, substantial time and good recovery [1][2]. Limited direct ab work and slower progress while dieting are noted as drawbacks [1].
No studies found of PHAT itself. Reviews of resistance training generally study volume and frequency, not this named program.

A looksmax.org thread recommends PHAT to skinny members seeking to gain size [3]. Norton's program is also referenced on T Nation training logs, where lifters report following it after other routines.
